Detachment is grief porn disguised as a character study of one of the most depressing people to ever live. I can’t remember the last time I hated a movie this much. No surprise that the doofus who made American History X thinks that this pseudo-tearjerker has anything substantial to say about teaching or education or socioeconomically disadvantaged kids. There is little to no reprieve from the sob stories depicted on screen which build on each other in such an unserious way that you can’t help but laugh by the end. A movie that was made to be clipped and shown in health classrooms and for teachers whose entire personality is their self-inflicted Sisyphean career choices.

Adrien Brody was the only thing that kept me from detaching myself from this movie. They tried to fit every possible form of human trauma into 98 mins and then kept shoving it in my face like 'look how deep it is'. the problem is that it was portrayed so badly that i feel like i suffered more watching this movie than the characters did🫩

Let’s actually be serious here, let’s not be all nerdy and discuss the ‘imagery’ and the ‘mood’ of the film. It absolutely sucks. It gets me thinking like who thinks this will entertain an audience? It’s so depressing it’s so uninspiring I just don’t understand the purpose of producing a film like this like I don’t gain anything from it except that a teacher’s life is utterly miserable apparently. I thought it was going to be like a Coach Carter storyline to it but it’s far from it. There was about 2 scenes where he inspired and engaged with the kids and that is the only joy in the film. Apart from the ending where he sees Erica, which is still unsolved it doesn’t actually say if he adopts her or not. Just so tragic to watch on a Sunday evening.

Detachment فيلم Detachment (2011) يتابع معلّمًا بديلًا يعيش حالة من الانفصال العاطفي عن العالم من حوله، محاولًا أداء عمله في مدرسة تعاني من الإهمال والفوضى. وبينما يواجه طلابًا مضطربين ونظامًا تعليميًا يفتقر إلى الأمل، تتكشف تدريجيًا جروحه الداخلية وشعوره العميق بالوحدة. الفيلم تأمل قاتم ومؤثر في العزلة، الاكتئاب، فقدان الأمل، وتأثير الإنسان في الآخرين رغم عجزه عن إنقاذ نفسه

Un Casting de malade pour un film nul à chier. On sent bien que le réalisateur se dit "Wow je fais un film tellement poétique". Je mets 1/5 parce que j'adore James Caan, mais c'est giga merdique. Tout les plans où Adrian Brody parle seul face cam, tu peux tout couper ça sert à rien et c'est pas si poétique que ça veux s'en donner l'air. Ça veux traiter 1000 sujets en même temps du coup tout est mal fait et c'est nul. La grosse de la classe qui se fait bully, on se dit que c'est parce qu'elle est grosse et un peu différente, mais en faite c'est une giga cassos, qui va carrément mettre en scène son suicide à la fin. Toute les minis histoires de l'histoire sont mal branlé et on pas de sens. Je vais pas détaillé parce que comme tout est nul y a même pas besoin. Gâché un casting pareil, surtout après avoir fait American History X c'est une folie incompréhensible. Edit: on est 2 semaines plus tard et je pense encore aux scènes avec la prostituée, qui joue vraiment très bien. Donc au final ça m'a quand même un peu marqué, et c'est sûrement la meilleure partie du film. J'augmente un peu ma note.

Detachment, directed by Tony Kaye of American History X fame, follows Adrien Brody's Henry, a drifting substitute teacher who struggles to inspire the students to take an interest in their education, as the educational system around him and his colleagues crumbles. A traditional setup in a lot of ways, but Detachment separates itself through its script and its editing, a mismatch of filmmaking styles, and a multitude of different character perspectives. The result is a relentless whirlwind of misery that, despite its best efforts, I failed to connect with. Detachment was written by Carl Lund, an interesting figure in the film industry, with only one writing credit to this day. What we do know, however, is that he used to be a public-school teacher, which quickly becomes apparent through this script — a raw and direct story that clearly comes from a place of personal rage and frustration. The movie is heavily critical of the state of the educational system, with each character serving as a vessel that represents a different struggle. Whether it be pressures from budget cuts, parents' unrealistic expectations of the school, or children with a struggling home life, it's all in here in one big — depressing — package. The result is a very nihilistic movie that offers little to no hope in its story. I'm not opposed to bleakness in film — Mike Leigh's Naked (1993), a British classic, also happens to be drenched in bleakness, with characters that embody the darkest outlooks on life, with little to no hope to be found. Detachment presents itself in a similar vein but lacks the narrative focus found in Leigh's classic. The movie clocks in at around one hour and thirty minutes but features multiple perspectives from a wide array of characters, which it struggles to juggle. There is a talented ensemble cast curated here, but most of the runtime is dedicated to Brody's character. Brody is competent in the role, but it was never clear why this character was the focal point — he's not a particularly likeable character, and even in moments where he does a good deed, he does so with a dejected and defeated energy, making him feel predictable and unengaging. Marcia Gay Harden's character felt like the more interesting focal point, with her pressures kicking off the story. Not only was her character more intriguing, but with the movie covering multiple teachers, students, and parents, her character being the headteacher would have made for a much better narrative framework to connect all these characters and bring a more natural focus. The juggling nature of Detachment also carries through into its filmmaking. Tonally, as we cut between Brody's shift in the classroom and his extracurricular miseries, the film switches from dreamlike, surreal composition — like that of a Terrence Malick film — to a more grounded, documentarian shooting style. Both styles feel at odds with each other and never come together in a satisfying way. Chaotic energy is part of the film's DNA, and the editing does a lot to feed that through: fast-paced cutting, continuity errors, intercutting between perspectives. Some may argue that this is an intentional choice given the themes, but after a while it becomes overbearing. Heat's (1995) famous bank-robbery shootout scene hits as hard as it does not just because the action is so exhilarating, but also because the editing kicks into a different gear. The moment works because the edit contrasts with the rest of the film — Detachment never allows itself that same contrast. With so many different characters and perspectives, all rendered in that same frantic style, there's nothing to alleviate the gloom. What can't be argued is that Detachment comes from a place of real conviction. Carl's script is full of despair and rage, and the themes of his writing have been successfully translated to the screen. However, I just wish the film had a little more restraint.

This film is often poorly acted, amateurishly shot in a way I don't personally like, and written rather weakly. It loses me a lot on the emotional aspects because it feels like it's trying too hard sometimes and yet simultaneously not hard enough to make me feel things. It's also sometimes a little sexist and racist if you think about it. Having said all that, I do appreciate the very honest grit this film has. It has some charm in spite of my dislike of certain aspects. It's an honesty I want more of from all art, and a vulnerability to tell something meaningful regardless of if you have the craftsmanship to see it through fully. It failed but it did so earnestly, I think that's worth something. While this story may be pretentious, I am posttentious. All things considered, I would recommend it. Detachment hooked me with its premise, but unfortunately, it didn’t quite hold up with its own narrative. While it tackled important themes like trauma, isolation, and the struggles within the education system, it ended up feeling like a string of tragic subplots being ticked off a checklist rather than one cohesive story. There was so much going on that I kept asking myself, “What’s happening? What’s this even about?” As the film kept introducing new tragedies without giving any of them enough time to fully resonate, I found myself becoming less and less invested. It became so dependent on piling on misery to make its point that, for me, it completely lost the emotional impact it was aiming for.

If you like overdoses, close-up shots, misery-porn, and actual good looking cinematography go watch requiem for a dream. Tony kaye has made 2 feature films (that are findable to watch) and this was his second one. I was a big fan of American history X. Also set in school (sometimes) and with a teacher. I liked American history x for it's realistic look and it's bold attempt at creating empathy for characters that shouldn't really deserve it. Detachment just shows miserable characters and is sometimes even laughably bad. I even laughed during the montage and the overdose scene. Overdose? More like overdoze! Tony Kaye has just proved to me that he isn't a good director or scriptwriter. In American history x, he was reportedly mad at Edward Norton for changing the script. Now I feel like he was actually the brains behind the film and characters of American history x. I actually did quite enjoy the first 30 minutes or so because of the documentary-style and the genius Adrien Brody. But it fell apart really quick. The social connections that were meant to be formed, felt incredibly lazy and unrealistic. For some reason every single woman in the film had to be naked or related to sex. Even the ginger teacher got spat on and why was there a naked grandma. What did this possibly add to the plot? That Henry isn't the only one with a demented parent? If I had a camcorder, and Adrien Brody. I would have made a 10 times better film.

The degree of ambivalence that i feel towards this movie cant be overstated. Its the equivalent of shaking you for 98 minutes and going "isnt it bad? Isnt it bad when bad things happen???" Without really offering anything to do in the face of adversity. It is true that we live in a world with a gutted education system and i imagine many teachers are finding themselves in a position thats at least a bit as sad as the main character. I dont think that misery porn is a solution tho. Overall, this is the movie equivalent of witnessing a car crash: you go "damn" and then you move on

I saw tiktok edits of this movie and decided I’ll give it a watch because I loved Adrien Brody’s character in Peaky Blinders and I think he’s a good actor. I do try my very best to watch movies with an open mind, and can appreciate when filmmakers take a more bold approach towards their craft. But this whole movie just felt like a misery porn that misses the mark, finding itself outside of what I assumed they were trying to go for. I’ve given this movie 2 tries and was just waiting for the movie to end both times. While I do understand why Tony Kaye chose to shoot the film in a handheld documentary-esque way, I just don't feel like it fits the way some people have said. Maybe my palette for cinema just isnt developed, But it makes me a bit sad to give this a low rating considering how much I really like Lucy Liu, Bryan Cranston, and Adrien Brody. I will eventually come around to watching this a third time because I do think this movie deserves an extra chance. Unfortunately at the current moment, Detachment will sit at a 2-star rating.
